paras: The lynching at Ponchatoula was the hanging of an unnamed Black man near Ponchatoula, Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana, on the night of February 8, 1888. Accused of breaking into a white man's house and assaulting his young daughter, he was taken from officers who were bringing him to the parish jail and was hanged to a tree. A New Orleans dispatch counted it as the second lynching in Tangipahoa Parish within ten days, and the placard left on the body, "We Protect Our Women," served as the headline over the story in at least two papers.

Ponchatoula lay on the Jackson railroad in Tangipahoa Parish, whose jail was at Amite City. It came within ten days of another lynching in the parish of a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, according to the New Orleans wire. Reports described the Ponchatoula man as "a stranger in that neighborhood," and the New Orleans wire said he was "claimed to be an escaped convict."

According to a special dispatch from Ponchatoula, a Black man forced his way into the house of Albert Tunnage on Sunday night, February 5, and assaulted his daughter. The New Orleans wire added that he entered the young woman's room with a hatchet and that a watchdog woke her father, while the Picayune's first report spoke only of an attempted assault six miles from town. He was caught and, in the Picayune correspondent's words, "fully identified."

The prisoner was held at Ponchatoula until officers set out to take him by train to the jail at Amite City. As they were about to board, "a squad of thirty men" took him from the officers, and the next morning his body was found hanging from a tree. The Picayune's correspondent credited the hanging to "regulators," while the New Orleans wire described "an armed gang of young white and negro men" who pinned a placard reading "We Protect Our Women" to his breast.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the lynchers was named.

The news reached the wire through a Ponchatoula special to the New Orleans Picayune, which the Richmond Dispatch ran on February 10 under "Strung Up by Regulators" and the Savannah Morning News as "Strung Up by Regulars"; a Baltimore German-language daily carried it the same day. A fuller Ponchatoula special appeared in a Michigan weekly on February 16, and the New Orleans wire of February 11 ran in Nebraska and Dakota papers under the placard's words.

Most papers reduced the story to a line in a news-briefs column. These briefs garbled the names: the Sacramento Daily Record-Union called the lynched man "Albert Tinage," the name others gave the girl's father, and a Forrest City, Arkansas, paper called him "an unknown negro." The same item ran in Martinsburg, West Virginia, a week after it appeared in Maysville, Kentucky.

Several papers openly approved. The Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford, Kentucky, called the man a "black brute" and stated as fact that he had "ravished" the young woman. A "Southern Gleanings" column, printed in Arkansas, Mississippi, Tennessee and Louisiana weeklies between February 16 and 18, ended its one-sentence notice with "The punishment fitted his crime."

Accounts differ on how the man came to the lynchers: the Picayune special said he escaped and was pursued and captured, the two fuller accounts said he was seized from officers at the train, and the Kentucky brief said he was taken from the jail. The girl's family is named Turney, Burney, Tunnage, Tunage, Tunago and, in the New Orleans wire, Nash. The dated Picayune dispatch put the hanging on the night of February 8, while the Sacramento brief said Thursday, February 9.

reader.title: Lynching at Ponchatoula, 1888
bases: An accused Black man was taken from officers or an escorting party by an armed group and hanged to a tree at Ponchatoula (A2, A8, A10).

The man was hanged by 'regulators', 'a squad of thirty men' or 'an armed gang' who seized him from the officers taking him to the parish jail, after he was accused of assaulting or attempting to assault a young white woman; a placard read 'We Protect Our Women' (A2, A8, A10).

Three separately worded dispatches, the Picayune's Ponchatoula special of Feb. 9, a fuller Ponchatoula special and a New Orleans wire of Feb. 11, agree that a Black man accused of an assault on a young woman was hanged by a group near Ponchatoula (A2, A8, A10).

accounts.label: Picayune's Ponchatoula special (Feb. 9)
accounts.gist: A Black man attempted to assault Bud Turney's daughter six miles from Ponchatoula, escaped, was pursued, captured and identified, and 'regulators' hanged him in the town the night before.

accounts.label: Ponchatoula special (fuller version)
accounts.gist: After a Sunday-night entry into Albert Tunnage's house, the man was arrested and held at Ponchatoula; as officers were boarding the train to take him to the Amite City jail, thirty men took him, and his body was found hanging the next morning.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire (Feb. 11)
accounts.gist: A claimed escaped convict forced his way with a hatchet into Miss Alberta Nash's room; caught and identified, he was seized from the party taking him to the Amite jail by an armed gang of young white and negro men, hanged, and labeled 'We Protect Our Women.' It called this the second Tangipahoa lynching in ten days.

accounts.label: Kentucky brief
accounts.gist: A 'black brute' who broke into a young lady's room and 'ravished' her was taken from the jail and hung by a mob.

framing.detail: The Southern Gleanings item, run in Arkansas, Mississippi, Tennessee and Louisiana weeklies, closed 'The punishment fitted his crime.'
The Stanford, Ky., paper called the man a 'black brute' and stated the rape as fact.
The New Orleans wire ran under the mob's own slogan, 'We Protect Our Women', calling the man 'the culprit' and the placard 'customary'.
Telegraphic briefs gave one line each, naming the charge as the reason for the lynching.
